title-group.article-title: Dyspnea during exercise and voluntary hyperpnea in women with obesity

abstract.p: Temporal responses of ratings of perceived breathlessness (RBP) during constant-load and incremental exercise, and during voluntary hyperpnea (EVH) were examined in obese women. Following 6min of constant-load (60W) cycling, 34 women rated RPB≥4 (+DOE) and 22 women rated RPB≤2 (−DOE). Both groups completed an incremental cycling test and an EVH test at 40 and 60L/min; RPB was assessed each minute of incremental cycling and at the end of each EVH trial. RPB increased with ventilation during constant-load (+DOE: R2=0.86; −DOE: R2=0.82) and incremental (+DOE: R2=0.91; −DOE: R2=0.92) exercise, but +DOE had a greater y-intercept than −DOE (60W: −0.16±1.53 vs −0.73±0.55; incremental: −0.50±1.40 vs −1.71±0.84). Despite matching ventilation, RPB was greater in +DOE at baseline (0.97±1.14 vs 0.14±0.28), 40L/min (2.50±1.43 vs 0.98±0.91), and 60L/min (3.94±2.19 vs 2.07±1.32) during EVH. These findings show that despite linear associations between RPB and ventilation during exercise and voluntary hyperpnea, breathlessness perception at a given ventilatory demand is heightened in +DOE compared with −DOE.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Obesity is associated with numerous health problems (Alpert, 2001; Azagury & Lautz, 2011; Ayinapudi et al., 2018) and exerts limitations to breathing capacity including decreased pulmonary function (Babb et al., 1989; DeLorey et al., 2005; El-Gamal et al., 2005) and altered respiratory mechanics (Babb et al., 2002; DeLorey et al., 2005; Lorenzo & Babb, 2013). These effects could provoke dyspnea on exertion (−DOE), which is a very common symptom in obesity (Gibson, 2000; Ofir et al., 2007; Babb et al., 2008a). However, not all individuals with obesity appear to experience DOE. Indeed, we have shown that during submaximal constant-load exercise, some otherwise healthy women with obesity experience dyspnea on exertion (+DOE) whereas others do not (−DOE) (Babb et al., 2008a).

At present, it remains unclear as to what mechanism(s) underlie the different ratings of perceived breathlessness (RPB; an indicator of DOE) in women with obesity. We have conducted several studies investigating possible mechanisms underlying differences between women with and without DOE, including investigations into the oxygen cost of breathing (Babb et al., 2008a), breathing mechanics and/or breathing pattern (Babb et al., 2008a), qualitative descriptors of respiratory sensations (Bernhardt & Babb, 2014), fat distribution (Babb et al., 2008b), and cardiorespiratory fitness and/or exercise capacity (Lorenzo & Babb, 2012). However, we note that these prior studies have reported only the RPB that has been identified during the final minute of a 6 min submaximal constant-load cycling test (performed at 60 W). That is, distinctions between +DOE (RPB ≥4) and −DOE (RPB ≤2) in these prior studies are made based upon a single RPB measurement during exercise at the same absolute work rate. Thus, the dynamic adjustment of RPB, either as a function of changes in relative exercise intensity or changes in ventilatory demand over time, has not been investigated in women with obesity. Given the temporal dynamics of respiratory sensations (Moosavi et al., 2004), it could be even more important to investigate the dynamic response of RPB. Indeed, investigating the dynamic response of RPB could be more representative of the individual’s perception of the overall exercise/ventilatory challenge, provide important insights into the origins of the dyspneic sensations, and/or help explain why some otherwise healthy women with obesity experience DOE and others do not. Moreover, it is currently unknown whether the dynamic response of RPB with exercise is related to exercise intensity, ventilatory demand, or a combination of both in women with obesity.

Therefore, the purpose of the present study was to explore the dynamic response of RBP during constant-load and incremental exercise, as well as at various levels of eucapnic voluntary hyperpnea (EVH). We assessed RPB during EVH to negate any potential confounding influence of exercise intensity on sensations of dyspnea when ventilatory demand was elevated. We retrospectively evaluated subjects’ RPB throughout both submaximal constant-load and incremental exercise (during which ventilation [V.E] was changing continuously), as well as at similar ventilatory demands during EVH in the same large group of participants as we have reported on previously (Bernhardt & Babb, 2014; Bernhardt et al., 2016).

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The data presented in this article were collected as part of a larger study describing the effects of weight loss on pulmonary function and breathing mechanics during exercise in women with obesity (Bernhardt & Babb, 2014; Bernhardt et al., 2016). However, the current article addresses a different question, and we repeat only the methods and data (i.e., subject characteristics, peak exercise data, and dyspnea ratings during exercise and EVH) essential to the novel findings presented here.

sec.title: Participants:
sec.p: In total, 78 women with obesity (body mass index [BMI] ≥30 and ≤45) were retrospectively examined. Participants were eligible to participate if they did not have a history of smoking, asthma, cardiovascular disease, sleep disorders, or musculoskeletal abnormalities that would preclude exercise. Prior to all testing, the purpose and protocols of all testing procedures were disclosed in detail and written and informed clinical consent was obtained. The experimental procedures were reviewed and approved by the UT Southwestern Institutional Review Board (Reference no: STU122010-108).

sec.title: Study design:
sec.p: Participants visited the laboratory on three separate occasions. On the first visit, participants underwent initial screening, standard anthropometric and body composition measures, and pulmonary function testing (data not shown) (Bernhardt & Babb, 2014). On the second visit, participants completed submaximal constant-load and maximal incremental cycling tests, and on the third visit participants completed EVH testing.

sec.title: Body composition and pulmonary function:
sec.p: Height and weight were recorded using calibrated scales, and body circumferences (waist and hips) were obtained. Hydrostatic weighing was performed as described previously to determine percent body fat, lean body mass, and total body fat mass (Babb et al., 2008a; Bernhardt & Babb, 2014). All participants completed pulmonary function testing (model 6200 body plethysmograph; SensorMedics, Yorba Linda, CA) including standard spirometry, lung volume, and diffusing capacity. Pulmonary function testing was performed according to American Thoracic Society guidelines (Miller et al., 2005).

sec.title: Submaximal constant-load cycling test:
sec.p: Before the exercise test, participants were given detailed written instructions for rating the intensity of perceived breathlessness (RPB; 0-10 Borg scale) as we have described previously (Bernhardt & Babb, 2014). Exercise testing began with participants seated on an upright electronically braked cycle ergometer (Lode Corival; Lode BV, Groningen, the Netherlands) with 3 min of resting baseline measurements after which a 6 min constant-load cycling test at 60 W was initiated. This exercise work rate (WR) was chosen based on prior studies on women with obesity who obtained ventilatory threshold at approximately 60 W (DeLorey et al., 2005). RPB was collected using the modified Borg scale (Borg, 1982) every 2 minutes, and the last value recorded was used to partition participants into +DOE and −DOE groups (see data and statistical analysis section for details). Heart rate (HR) and blood pressure, as well as pulmonary gas exchange variables including V.E, oxygen uptake (V.O2), and carbon dioxide elimination (V.CO2) were measured using the Douglas bag technique. Expired volume was measured using a 200 L Tissot spirometer and gas fractions were measured using a mass spectrometer (Perkin-Elmer 1100). Flow was measured continuously using an inspiratory pneumotachograph (Hans Rudolph, Model 4813) and a heated expiratory pneumotachograph (Hans Rudolph, model 3850A) connected to a Hans Rudolph valve (Model 2700) via large-bore tubing. Flow signals were combined into a single bidirectional flow signal (Validyne Buffer Amplifier, model BA112) and digitally integrated to yield volume, breathing frequency (Fb) and tidal volume (VT).

sec.title: Maximal incremental cycling test:
sec.p: Following the submaximal constant-load cycling test and a brief resting period, participants performed a maximal incremental cycling test on the same upright cycle ergometer to determine peak exercise capacity. After resting baseline measurements were acquired, participants started cycling at 60-65 rpm with an initial WR of 20 W. The WR was increased by 20 W each minute (using a stepwise protocol) until the participant reached volitional exhaustion. Maximal effort was evidenced by approaching predicted peak HR, peak WR, peak oxygen uptake (V.O2peak), and/or a respiratory exchange ratio >1.1. RPB was collected at rest and at the end of each stage of exercise throughout the incremental cycling test. Pulmonary gas exchange variables were measured as described above for the submaximal constant-load cycling test.

sec.title: Eucapnic voluntary hyperpnea (EVH) test:
sec.p: While seated upright, subjects completed 6 min of baseline rest followed by 4 min of EVH at both 40 and 60 L/min as previously described (Babb et al., 2008a). The order in which the levels of EVH were conducted was randomized, except for rest, which was always measured first. Participants breathed from a 1,000 L inspiratory reservoir bag containing 4% (used at 40 L/min) or 5% (used at 60 L/min) CO2 (21% O2 and balance N2) to maintain eucapnia (Babb et al., 2008a). RPB was obtained during the last 30s of each stage (i.e., rest, and at 40 and 60 L/min), whereas HR, V.E, and V.O2 were averaged from the 6 min measurements at rest and final 2 min measurements during the EVH maneuvers. Pulmonary gas exchange variables were measured as described above for the submaximal constant-load cycling test.

sec.title: Data and statistical analysis:
sec.p: Participants were assigned to one of three groups according to their RPB during minute 6 of the submaximal constant-load cycling test. In keeping with previous studies (Babb et al., 2008; Bernhardt & Babb, 2014a; Bernhardt & Babb, 2014b), those with RPB ≤2 were designated as women without DOE (i.e., −DOE) and those with RPB ≥4 were designated as women with DOE (i.e., +DOE). Those women with an RPB of 3 were excluded to better delineate differences between the +DOE and −DOE groups. Therefore, the participants who had an RPB of 3 did not perform maximal incremental cycling exercise or EVH tests. The establishment of these groups was based on our previous finding that women with obesity have an average RPB of 2±1 at the ventilatory threshold during incremental exercise (DeLorey et al., 2005). Anthropometric differences between +DOE and −DOE groups were determined by independent t-tests. A two-way mixed analysis of variance was performed to determine differences in ventilatory and dyspnea measures during across time (exercise and EVH levels) and between groups (+DOE and −DOE). Post-Hoc (Bonferroni) comparisons were used to adjust for multiple testing. Linear regression analyses were performed on each participant and the mean values were reported to describe the relationship between RPB and V.E. Changes in RPB during the maximal incremental cycling test were modelled using a simple exponential regression of the form: y=aeb*x where y represents RPB, a represents the predicted y-intercept, b represents the curvature constant, and x represents the relative exercise intensity (i.e., HR reserve, determined as [observed HR − baseline HR] / [maximal HR − baseline HR] * 100 (Garet et al., 2005). This exponential regression model has previously been used to describe changes in V.E as a function of increasing exercise intensity (Baba et al., 2002). Statistical significance was accepted at p < 0.05.

Individual (pooled) RPB as a function of changing V.E (bottom panel) during submaximal constant-load 60 W cycling with linear regression models superimposed. Regression lines were calculated from the average y-intercept and slope estimates from the regression analysis within each individual. *Significantly different from −DOE, p < 0.05; †Significantly different from +DOE at minute 2, p < 0.05 (denoted by dashed line).

fn.p: Data are presented as mean ± SD. +DOE denotes obese women with dyspnea on exertion (RPB ≥ 4); −DOE denotes obese women with only mild dyspnea on exertion (RPB ≤ 2).

list-item.p: Changes in RPB during exercise or EVH are in linear proportion to changes in V.E.
RPB at a given V.E is elevated in obese women with vs. without dyspnea on exertion.
Obese women with dyspnea on exertion experience increased perception for a given V.E.
